question: In 2023, the owner of the Château Bessan-Ségur vineyard and winery brought a case before the Commercial Court in Bordeaux against buyers – in this case, Ginestat and Excell – for failure to fulfil their obligation to pay a price that covers the cost of production. This obligation is laid down in France’s EGAlim law1.

The case caused an uproar because it could have huge consequences for the French agri-food sector and could set a precedent for the sector in other Member States such as Spain, where the winegrowers of the Autonomous Community of Rioja charge less than the cost of production.

By finding against Ginestat and Excell and fining them for buying wine at unfairly low prices, the Commercial Court set a precedent, as it was the first tribunal to invoke the EGAlim law since it came into force in 2019. 1.
Is the Commission planning to align EU legislation with the obligations laid down in the EGAlim law?

What measures is the Commission considering to alleviate the plight of European winegrowers, whose sales are falling and who are structurally at a disadvantage when negotiating prices with distributors?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2024) One of the key objectives of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) is to reinforce the position of farmers in the food supply chain.

In March 2024, the Commission presented at the AGRIFISH Council meeting a reflection paper on actions to improve the situation through reinforced contractualisation, extended mediation mechanisms and other measures that would also benefit the wine sector.

Actions to ensure that buyers pay a price covering production costs should be assessed against their impact on farmers’ competitiveness and productivity, as well as against the risk of maintaining or creating oversupply. In addition, selling below cost is sometimes the only viable option for farmers in the short run to minimize their losses and not to lose their products.

The Commission launched a study to better understand the impact of such measures. The issue may be examined in more details looking into the CAP post 2027. The EU has already adopted measures to address the vulnerable position of farmers on the supply chain, like the prohibition of certain abusive behaviours by the Directive on unfair trading practices in the food supply chain1 (UTP).

A recent report on the implementation of this directive will feed into a thorough evaluation in 2025, which may lead to specific legislative proposals. As a first action of the above-mentioned reflection paper, an observatory of production costs, margins and trading practices in the agri-food supply chain has been created, to increase transparency and build trust in the chain.
